adultDose: 2.4 mg/kg IV or IM at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then once daily until oral therapy tolerated
pediatricDose: Children weighing < 20 kg: 3 mg/kg per dose (higher mg/kg than adults) at the same 0, 12, 24h then daily schedule. Children >= 20 kg: same as adult, 2.4 mg/kg.
notes: Where IV/IM artesunate is unavailable and the child is under 6 years, a single pre-referral rectal dose (10 mg/kg) may be given before urgent transfer; rectal artesunate should not be used in older children or adults.
contraindications: None absolute in severe malaria given mortality risk; monitor for post-artesunate delayed hemolysis in the 2-4 weeks after treatment.

adultDose: Weight-band dosing PO BID x 3 days (6 doses total at 0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60h), taken with a fat-containing meal
pediatricDose: Weight-band dosing, same schedule as adult, tablet strength varies by weight band
notes: WHO-recommended ACT options include artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, and artesunate-pyronaridine. In the first trimester of pregnancy, artemether-lumefantrine is preferred where no safer alternative exists. A single low dose of primaquine (0.25 mg/kg) can be added to reduce transmission in low-transmission settings.
contraindications: Check for known hypersensitivity; verify choice of ACT against local resistance patterns.

adultDose: Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 7 days (or per WHO 2024 evidence-based first-line status; some protocols use a 1g loading dose on day 1 then 500mg daily). If parenteral needed: Ceftriaxone 2-4 g IV once daily.
pediatricDose: Azithromycin 20 mg/kg PO once daily for 5-7 days. Ceftriaxone 75-80 mg/kg IV once daily if parenteral needed.
notes: As of WHO's 2024 evidence review, azithromycin is now favored as first-line over fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance (exceeding 70% in South Asia) and superior relapse/failure rates versus older options. Ciprofloxacin should not be used as empiric first-line unless local resistance data confirms susceptibility.
contraindications: Avoid fluoroquinolones empirically in high-resistance settings; verify local antibiogram where available.

condition: Suspected or probable acute bacterial meningitis
adultDose: Ceftriaxone at maximum dosage, administered every 12 hours in inpatient settings (once-daily acceptable only in large-scale epidemic settings if the same total daily dose is maintained). Dexamethasone (or hydrocortisone/methylprednisolone if unavailable) started with the first antibiotic dose, typically on a 6-hourly schedule.
pediatricDose: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime at maximum weight-based dosage q12h; corticosteroid timing as above. Add ampicillin or amoxicillin if risk factors for Listeria monocytogenes.
notes: This is WHO's first-ever global meningitis guideline (April 2025), which supersedes the meningitis section of the 2022 AWaRe antibiotic book. During confirmed meningococcal epidemics: ceftriaxone x 5 days. During confirmed pneumococcal epidemics: consider ceftriaxone x 10 days. Corticosteroid course should be guided by CSF findings once available; discontinue after 4 days if pathogen other than pneumococcus/H. influenzae confirmed.
contraindications: Add Listeria coverage (ampicillin) in age >50, pregnancy, or immunocompromise.
